content: Nocturnal enuresis, commonly referred to as bed-wetting, is a socially challenging and emotionally distressing condition that affects approximately 15% to 20% of five-year-old children and persists in up to 2% of young adults. Desmopressin, a synthetic analogue of vasopressin, has been studied as a treatment option for this condition. A systematic review of 47 randomized controlled trials, involving a total of 3,448 children (2,210 of whom received desmopressin), was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of desmopressin in managing nocturnal enuresis. The quality of many of these trials was suboptimal. The findings demonstrated that desmopressin was effective in reducing the frequency of bed-wetting episodes during the treatment period when compared to placebo. For instance, children receiving a 20 µg dose of desmopressin experienced an average reduction of 1.34 wet nights per week (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.11 to 1.57). Additionally, children treated with desmopressin were more likely to achieve dryness during the treatment phase. For example, in one analysis, 81% of children receiving desmopressin remained wet compared to 98% in the placebo group, with a relative risk (RR) of failure to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.79 to 0.91). However, the benefits of desmopressin were not sustained after the treatment was discontinued. There was no clear evidence of a dose-dependent effect of desmopressin, and the limited data comparing oral versus nasal administration were inconclusive. When compared to enuresis alarms, desmopressin showed no significant differences in efficacy during the treatment period in four small trials. However, alarms appeared to have a lower risk of failure or relapse after treatment cessation in two of these trials. Specifically, 65% of children using desmopressin experienced relapse or failure compared to 46% of those using alarms (RR: 1.42, 95% CI: 1.05 to 1.91). Combining desmopressin with alarm therapy resulted in fewer wet nights during treatment compared to alarms alone (weighted mean difference [WMD]: -0.83, 95% CI: -1.11 to -0.55). However, there were no significant differences in failure rates during treatment (RR: 0.88, 95% CI: 0.73 to 1.05) or relapse rates after treatment cessation (49% versus 55%; RR: 0.91, 95% CI: 0.76 to 1.08). When compared to tricyclic antidepressants, such as amitriptyline, desmopressin appeared to have similar efficacy during treatment. However, in two trials, children treated with imipramine were less likely to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights compared to those treated with desmopressin (RR: 0.44, 95% CI: 0.27 to 0.73). Tricyclics were associated with a higher incidence of side effects. Desmopressin may also be more effective than nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as diclofenac or indomethacin, although the evidence is limited. There was insufficient data to assess the relative efficacy of behavioral or complementary therapies compared to desmopressin. The authors concluded that desmopressin is effective in rapidly reducing the number of wet nights per week in children with nocturnal enuresis. However, the available evidence suggests that these benefits are not sustained after treatment discontinuation. While desmopressin and tricyclic antidepressants appear to have similar effects during treatment, enuresis alarms may provide more durable benefits. These conclusions are tentative due to the limited quality and quantity of evidence. To minimize the risk of water intoxication, children undergoing desmopressin treatment should be advised to restrict fluid intake to no more than 240 mL (8 ounces) during the evening prior to administration.
